title: Confident English & Communication for the Workplace
tagline: Speak English with confidence at work: fix common mistakes, handle calls, shine in interviews and meetings, and write polite, clear e-mails.
takeaways: Fix common tense and article errors
description:
Many people in Pakistan read and write English well, but freeze when they have to speak it. This course is for Urdu speakers who want to use English with confidence at work. It focuses on the English language itself: the phrases, grammar and sounds that make you clear, polite and easy to understand.

**Basic stages (free):**
- **Confidence and everyday English:** beat the fear of speaking, introduce yourself naturally and keep small talk going.
- **Common mistakes, fixed:** tenses, articles and prepositions that trouble many Urdu speakers, plus clear pronunciation habits.
- **Phone calls and polite requests:** answer calls, spell names, take messages and ask for things without sounding bossy.

**Advanced stages (Premium):**
- **Meetings and job interviews:** phrases for agreeing, disagreeing and interrupting, a strong self-introduction and the STAR method.
- **Presentations and persuasive speaking:** signposting, describing numbers and trends, using your voice and handling questions honestly.
- **Professional writing and difficult conversations:** clear e-mails, feedback, saying no, apologising and negotiating politely.

You follow Ayesha, Hamza and Bilal as they practise with their mentor Sana in Lahore, Karachi, Faisalabad and Islamabad. Every stage ends with a short test.
audience: Students and fresh graduates preparing for internships, interviews and their first job
Job seekers who understand English well but lose confidence when they have to speak it
Office staff who must answer calls, join meetings and write e-mails in English
Small-business owners and exporters who deal with customers and buyers abroad
Anyone who thinks in Urdu and wants English that sounds natural, not translated
outcomes: Introduce yourself and make small talk naturally, without word-for-word translation from Urdu
Correct common mistakes with tenses, articles, prepositions and question word order
Pronounce v and w, s-clusters and word stress clearly so listeners follow you easily
Handle work phone calls, spell names, take messages and make polite requests
Speak up in meetings and answer interview questions with a strong introduction and STAR stories
Present clearly with signposting and trend language, and persuade honestly
Write clear e-mails and give feedback, say no, apologise and negotiate politely

sessions.title: Finding Your Voice: Confidence and Everyday English
sessions.summary: Break the fear of speaking, greet people and introduce yourself naturally, keep small talk going, and swap word-for-word Urdu translations for phrases that sound natural in English.
objectives: Explain why fear of mistakes stops people speaking and use small daily habits to practise
Greet people and introduce yourself naturally in formal and informal situations
Keep a short small-talk conversation going with safe topics and follow-up questions
Replace common word-for-word translations from Urdu with natural English phrases

cards.title: I understand everything, but I can't speak
cards.setting: Sana's evening English club, a community hall in Gulberg, Lahore. Thursday, 7 p.m.

lines.text: Welcome to the Speaking Circle. Every Thursday, Sana Qureshi runs a free English practice club. Tonight three new members are sitting in the front row.
I did my BBA in English. I can read any report. But when someone speaks to me in English, my mind goes blank and I answer in one word.
Same here. My written assignments get good marks, but in my viva I froze. I was translating every sentence from Urdu in my head.
At our textile unit in Faisalabad, buyers from abroad call us. I always pass the phone to my manager. I'm scared they will laugh at my English.
Good news: none of you has a knowledge problem. You have a practice problem, and practice problems can be fixed.
Your first mission is simple. By next Thursday, each of you will introduce yourself to a stranger in English and keep the chat going for two minutes.

cards.title: Why we freeze, and how to unfreeze

scenes.heading: The fear of judgement
scenes.narration: Many of us were corrected loudly in school, so speaking English feels like a test. The brain treats the test as danger, and the words disappear. Knowing this is the first step.

scenes.heading: Translating in your head
scenes.narration: When you build each sentence in Urdu first and then translate it, you are doing two jobs at once. It is slow, and the result often sounds unnatural. Learning ready-made English phrases removes one job.

scenes.heading: The perfection trap
scenes.narration: Waiting until your sentence is perfect means you never speak. Listeners care far more about your message than about one wrong preposition.

scenes.heading: Practice builds speed
scenes.narration: Speaking is a skill like riding a bike. Short, regular practice, even ten minutes a day, makes words come faster than one long session a month.

scenes.heading: Clear beats perfect
scenes.narration: The goal is to be understood and to be polite, not to sound like a newsreader. A Pakistani accent is fine. Clear words, a calm pace and good manners are what people remember.

cards.title: The confidence ladder
cards.caption: Climb one step at a time. Each step is a little more public than the last.

items.label: Read aloud alone
items.detail: Read a news article or a page of a book aloud for five minutes a day.

items.label: Talk to yourself
items.detail: Describe what you are doing in English: 'I'm making tea. I'm checking my e-mail.'

items.label: Record and listen
items.detail: Record a one-minute voice note on your phone, listen back and note one thing to improve.

items.label: Speak with a friend
items.detail: Agree an 'English only' ten minutes with a friend or family member.

items.label: Speak in a small group
items.detail: Join a club or class where everyone is learning and mistakes are expected.

items.label: Speak at work
items.detail: Use one new phrase in a real meeting, call or chat each day.

cards.question: Sana tells the group what matters most when they speak English at work. Which statement matches her advice?
options: You should lose your Pakistani accent before speaking in meetings
Being understood and polite matters more than sounding perfect
It is better to stay quiet until you can speak without any mistakes
cards.explanation: Listeners focus on the message and the manners. An accent is normal and fine. Waiting for perfection simply means you never practise.

cards.title: Greetings and introductions that sound natural
cards.body:
How you start a conversation sets the tone. Keep it short and friendly.

**Formal (a manager, a client, an interview):** 'Good morning. I'm Ayesha Malik. It's a pleasure to meet you.'

**Informal (a colleague, a classmate):** 'Hi, I'm Ayesha. Nice to meet you.'

**Replying to 'How are you?':** 'I'm fine, thanks. And you?' or 'Good, thanks. How about you?' It is a greeting, not a medical question, so keep it short.

**Watch out for:** 'Myself Ayesha.' In standard English, *myself* cannot start a sentence like this. Say 'I'm Ayesha' or 'My name is Ayesha.'

**Asking a name politely:** 'Sorry, could I have your name?' or 'What's your name?' The phrase 'What is your good name?' is a direct translation of 'Aap ka naam?' and sounds odd to many international listeners.

cards.title: Translated from Urdu or natural English?
cards.caption: The words on the left are understood in Pakistan, but they can confuse people from other countries.

items.label: Introducing yourself
items.right: I'm Ayesha. / My name is Ayesha.

items.label: Asking a name
items.right: Could I have your name, please?

items.label: Asking for action
items.right: Could you please send me the form?

cards.front: At the start of a meeting
cards.back: 'How was your weekend?' or 'Did you have far to come today?'
'How are you finding the new job so far?'

cards.back: 'How do you know the bride and groom?'

cards.front: Waiting for a lift or a bus
cards.back: 'The traffic was terrible on the canal road today. How was your journey?'
'Did you do anything nice over the holiday?'

cards.front: With a visitor to your city
cards.back: 'Is this your first time in Lahore? Have you tried any of the food yet?'

cards.prompt: Sort each topic for small talk with someone you have just met at work.

items.text: The weather or the traffic
Weekend plans or a recent holiday
Food and favourite places to eat
A cricket match everyone watched
How much they earn
Their political or religious views
'When are you getting married?'
Comments about their weight or looks

cards.title: Meeting a visitor at a seminar
cards.situation: Ayesha is at a careers seminar at a Lahore university. During the tea break, a visiting manager from a software company in Dubai stands next to her at the tea table. She has never spoken to him before. What should she do?

choices.text: Smile and say: 'Hi, I'm Ayesha. I've just finished my BBA. Are you enjoying the seminar so far?'
choices.outcome: He smiles, introduces himself as Imran and says the second talk was the best. Ayesha asks what he liked about it. A short, easy chat follows, and he gives her his card. A friendly greeting, her name and an open question did all the work.

choices.text: Say: 'Myself Ayesha, BBA. What is your good name, sir?'
choices.outcome: He understands her and is polite, but the phrases sound translated and the conversation feels stiff. The intention was good; the wording made it harder to relax.

choices.text: Stay silent and look at her phone in case she makes a mistake
choices.outcome: The chance passes. Silence feels safe, but it never builds confidence. A short, imperfect greeting would have been far better than none.

cards.title: Ayesha's 30-second introduction
cards.body:
Sana teaches the group a simple shape for introducing yourself: **present, past, future.**

- **Present:** 'Hi, I'm Ayesha Malik. I'm a business graduate from Lahore.'
- **Past:** 'I did my BBA at a university here, and I did a three-month internship in a bank's marketing team.'
- **Future:** 'Now I'm looking for my first full-time role in digital marketing.'

Then she hands the conversation back: **'What about you? What brings you here today?'**

It takes about 30 seconds, it is easy to remember, and it ends with a question so the other person can talk too.

cards.title: Choose the natural reply
cards.prompt: Match each thing someone says with a natural reply.

pairs.left: 'Thank you so much for your help.'

cards.question: Hamza's new classmate asks, 'How was your weekend?' Which reply keeps the conversation going best?
options: 'Really nice, thanks. I went to Clifton beach with my cousins. How was yours?'
'Fine.'
'It was fine. Why are you asking me about my weekend?'
cards.explanation: A good reply answers, adds one small detail and passes a question back. 'Fine.' closes the conversation, and asking why sounds defensive.

cards.title: The 'answer plus one' habit
cards.body:
When someone asks you a question, give your answer **plus one** small detail, and then ask something back.

'Where are you from?' becomes: 'I'm from Multan, **but I've lived in Lahore for three years. Where are you from?**'

This one habit turns a quick question into a real conversation, and it gives the other person something to reply to.

cards.title: Keep a small-talk chat going
cards.prompt: Put the steps of a short, friendly conversation with someone new into a natural order.
steps: Greet and say your name: 'Hi, I'm Bilal.'
Ask an easy, open question: 'How are you finding the exhibition?'
Listen, then ask a follow-up about their answer
Close politely: 'It was great talking to you. Enjoy the rest of the day.'

cards.title: Take-aways from the Speaking Circle
items: Freezing comes from fear and translating in your head, not from a lack of knowledge.
Practise little and often, and climb the confidence ladder one step at a time.
Clear and polite beats perfect. A Pakistani accent is fine.
Introduce yourself with 'I'm...' or 'My name is...', not 'Myself...'.
Use the present-past-future shape, then hand the conversation back with a question.
Stick to safe small-talk topics and use 'answer plus one' to keep a chat going.

cards.prompt: Which step of the confidence ladder are you on today? Write down one small thing you will do in English every day this week, and one phrase from this stage you will use tomorrow.

quiz.question: Ayesha understands English well but goes silent when she has to speak. According to Sana, what is the main cause?
options: A small vocabulary that needs thousands of new words before she can start
A lack of speaking practice combined with fear of making mistakes
Her Pakistani accent, which listeners cannot understand
Her BBA, which was taught in English and not in Urdu
quiz.explanation: Ayesha already knows plenty of English. The block is fear and too little practice, which regular, low-pressure speaking fixes.

quiz.question: Which introduction sounds most natural to an international listener?
options: 'Myself Hamza, doing computer science.'
'Myself is Hamza and I am doing the computer science.'
'Hamza myself, a student of the computer science.'
'Hi, I'm Hamza. I'm studying computer science.'
quiz.explanation: In standard English you introduce yourself with 'I'm...' or 'My name is...'. 'Myself' cannot start a sentence this way.

quiz.question: Someone at a seminar asks you, 'How are you?' What is the best kind of reply?
options: A short, friendly answer and a question back, such as 'Fine, thanks. And you?'
A full account of how your week has gone, including any health problems
No reply, because it is only a greeting and not a real question
A single word, 'Good,' and then you turn away to check messages on your phone
quiz.explanation: 'How are you?' is a greeting. A short answer plus a question back is polite and keeps the door open for more conversation.

quiz.question: Why can translating every sentence from Urdu in your head slow you down?
options: You are doing two jobs at once, and the result often sounds unnatural
Urdu and English have no words in common, so translation is impossible
English speakers can always tell when you are thinking in another language
Translating is only a problem for people who speak more than two languages
quiz.explanation: Building the sentence in Urdu and then translating it is slow work, and word-for-word translation creates phrases such as 'What is your good name?'. Learning ready-made English phrases removes one step.

quiz.question: Which of these is a safe small-talk topic with a colleague you have just met?
options: Their plans for the weekend
How much they earn in their new role
When they are planning to get married
Their views on the last election
quiz.explanation: Weekend plans are light and friendly. Salary, marriage plans and politics are personal or divisive and are best avoided with someone you have just met.

quiz.question: Which phrase is a natural way to ask someone's name politely?
options: 'What is your good name, please?'
'Tell me your good name.'
'Your name is what?'
'Sorry, could I have your name?'
quiz.explanation: 'Could I have your name?' is polite and natural. 'What is your good name?' is a direct translation from Urdu and can sound strange outside South Asia.

quiz.question: In the 'present, past, future' introduction, what goes in the 'future' part?
options: Where you were born, which school you attended and your favourite subjects
What you are aiming for next, such as the kind of job you want
Your current job title and the company where you work now
A question asking the listener where they studied
quiz.explanation: Present is who you are now, past is the relevant background and future is what you are working towards. You then hand over with a question.

quiz.question: Bilal is asked, 'Where are you from?' Which answer uses the 'answer plus one' habit?
options: 'Faisalabad.'
'I am from Faisalabad, which is a city.'
'I'm from Faisalabad. I work in a textile unit there. Where are you from?'
'Why do you want to know where I am from?'
quiz.explanation: 'Answer plus one' means giving the answer, one small extra detail and a question back. That gives the other person something to reply to.

quiz.question: Which daily habit is the lowest-pressure first step on the confidence ladder?
options: Giving a presentation to your whole department
Leading a client call in English on your first day
Reading a page aloud on your own for five minutes
Answering every question in a job interview in English
quiz.explanation: The ladder starts with private practice such as reading aloud. Public speaking at work comes later, once the earlier steps feel easy.

quiz.question: Your colleague says, 'Have a good weekend!' What is the most natural reply?
options: 'Thanks, you too!'
'Same to same!'
'Thank you, I will try my best.'
'Okay.'
quiz.explanation: 'Thanks, you too!' returns the good wishes naturally. 'Same to same' is not standard English, and 'Okay' sounds cold.

sessions.title: Fixing the Usual Mistakes: Tenses, Articles, Prepositions and Clear Sounds
sessions.summary: Fix the grammar mistakes that many Urdu speakers make in English, from tenses and articles to prepositions and questions, and build pronunciation habits that make your English clear and easy to follow.
objectives: Use present perfect with since and for, and avoid continuous forms with verbs such as know and have
Choose a, an, the or no article correctly in everyday sentences
Use common prepositions correctly and drop extra words such as 'discuss about' and 'return back'
Form direct and indirect questions in the correct word order
Pronounce v and w, s-clusters and word stress clearly

cards.title: The e-mail that came back with red ink
cards.setting: A small office in Model Town, Lahore, where Sana helps Ayesha check a cover letter. Saturday morning.

lines.text: Look. My cousin read my cover letter and circled six things in red. 'I am working here since 2023.' 'I am having good computer skills.' What is wrong with them?
Nothing is wrong with you. These are the most common mistakes Urdu speakers make, because Urdu builds those ideas differently. Once you see the pattern, you fix it everywhere.
My teacher always says 'Did you went?' is wrong, but it sounds right to me.
For me it is speaking. A buyer heard 'vest' when I said 'west', and we spent five minutes confused about a shipment.
Then today we go into the repair workshop. Six common grammar fixes and three sound habits. No rules for the sake of rules, only the ones that change how clear you are.

scenes.heading: Since and for
scenes.narration: Urdu often uses the present for something that started in the past and is still true. English uses the present perfect: 'I have been working here since 2023' or 'for two years'. Since is a starting point; for is a length of time.

scenes.heading: Thinking and having verbs
scenes.narration: Verbs for states, such as know, understand, want, like and have (owning something), are usually not used in the -ing form. Say 'I have good computer skills', not 'I am having'. 'I'm having lunch' is fine, because it is an action.

scenes.heading: After did, use the base form
scenes.narration: Did already shows the past, so the next verb stays simple: 'Did you go?' and 'I didn't see it.' Not 'Did you went?' or 'I didn't saw it.'

scenes.heading: Finished time means past simple
scenes.narration: If you name a finished time such as yesterday or last week, use the past simple: 'I saw him yesterday.' Save 'I have seen' for experiences without a time: 'I have seen that film.'

scenes.heading: He, she and it take -s
scenes.narration: In the present simple, add -s or -es after he, she and it: 'She works in sales.' 'He doesn't know.' Not 'He don't know.'

cards.title: Six grammar repairs
cards.caption: Each pair shows a common mistake and a correct version.

items.label: Since and for
items.right: I have been working here since 2023.

items.label: After did
items.left: Did you went to the office?
items.right: Did you go to the office?

items.label: Indirect questions
items.left: Can you tell me where is the bank?
items.right: Can you tell me where the bank is?

cards.question: Which sentence is correct?
options: I am living in Karachi since five years.
I live in Karachi since five years.
I have lived in Karachi since five years.
I have lived in Karachi for five years.
cards.explanation: Use the present perfect for a situation that started in the past and continues now, and use 'for' with a length of time. 'Since' needs a starting point, such as 'since 2021'.

cards.title: A, an, the or nothing?
cards.body:
Urdu has no words that work exactly like *a*, *an* and *the*, so articles are the trickiest part of English for many of us. Four simple rules cover most sentences.

- **Jobs and single countable things need a or an:** 'I am **an** engineer.' 'She has **a** car.' Not 'I am engineer.'
- **Choose a or an by sound, not spelling:** **an** hour, **an** MBA (it starts with an 'em' sound), **a** university (it starts with a 'yoo' sound), **a** one-day course.
- **Use the when both people know which one:** 'Please send **the** report I shared yesterday.' 'Can you open **the** door?'
- **Use no article for general ideas and plurals:** '**Life** is busy in Karachi.' '**Customers** want fast replies.' Not 'The life is busy.'

cards.title: A, an or the?
cards.prompt: Sort each gap into the article that fits. Read the sentence aloud to hear the first sound.

items.text: She is ___ accountant at a bank.
I need ___ hour to finish the report.
He studied at ___ university in Peshawar.
Bilal has ___ meeting at 3 p.m.
Can you send me ___ file you mentioned this morning?
Hamza is doing ___ MBA in the evenings.
Please close ___ window next to you.
Ayesha wants to become ___ marketing executive.

cards.title: Fix the preposition
cards.prompt: Match each mistake with the correct version.

pairs.right: 'I will return on Monday.' (return already means come back)

pairs.left: 'The meeting is on 5 p.m. in Monday.'
pairs.right: 'The meeting is at 5 p.m. on Monday.'

cards.title: At, on, in for time
cards.caption: From the most exact time at the top to the widest period at the bottom.

items.label: at
items.detail: Exact times: at 9 a.m., at lunchtime, at night

items.label: on
items.detail: Days and dates: on Monday, on 14 August, on my birthday

items.label: in
items.detail: Months, years, seasons and parts of the day: in March, in 2025, in summer, in the morning

cards.title: Bilal's message to a buyer
cards.situation: Bilal needs to send a short message to a buyer abroad. His draft says: 'Dear Sir, I am working in this company since 2019. The shipment will reach in Monday. Kindly discuss about price with me.' He asks Ayesha what to change before he sends it.

choices.text: Fix the three grammar points: 'I have been working here since 2019. The shipment will arrive on Monday. Could we discuss the price?'
choices.outcome: The message is now short, correct and polite. The buyer replies within an hour to agree a call. Small fixes made Bilal sound precise, which matters when money is involved.

choices.text: Change only 'Kindly' to 'Please' and leave the rest
choices.outcome: The tone is a little better, but the tense, preposition and 'discuss about' mistakes remain. The buyer still understands, but the message looks less professional than Bilal's work really is.

choices.text: Rewrite it as a long, very formal paragraph with difficult words to sound educated
choices.outcome: The buyer has to read it twice. Long, complicated sentences hide meaning and add new mistakes. Simple and correct is more professional than long and fancy.

cards.title: Three sound habits for clear English

scenes.heading: V and W are two different sounds
scenes.narration: Urdu uses one sound, often between v and w. In English they change meaning: vest and west, vine and wine. For v, touch your top teeth to your bottom lip. For w, round your lips like a kiss, with no teeth.

scenes.heading: No extra vowel before s-clusters
scenes.narration: Words like school, station and speak start with s plus another consonant. Many of us add a sound in front: 'iskool', 'isteshun'. Start directly with a long 'sss': sss-chool, sss-tation.

scenes.heading: Stress the right part of the word
scenes.narration: English makes one part of a word stronger. PHO-to-graph but pho-TO-gra-phy. de-VEL-op. COM-for-ta-ble, often said as three beats: COMF-ta-ble. Wrong stress confuses listeners more than a wrong vowel.

scenes.heading: Slow down and pause
scenes.narration: When we are nervous we speed up. Short pauses between ideas give listeners time to follow and give you time to think. Clear and calm is more professional than fast.

cards.back: v: top teeth on bottom lip. w: round lips, no teeth. A vest is clothing; west is a direction.
Start with a long s: 'sss-kool', not 'is-kool'.
PHO-to-graph (stress on the first part). pho-TO-gra-phy (stress on the second part).
de-VEL-op: the stress is in the middle.
Often said as three beats: VEJ-ta-bl.
fif-TEEN (stress at the end). FIF-ty (stress at the start). This matters for prices and quantities.

cards.question: Hamza says 'Where you are going?' to a classmate. What is the correct question?
options: Where are you going?
Where you going are?
Where are going you?
Where you are go?
cards.explanation: In direct questions the helping verb comes before the subject: 'Where are you going?' In indirect questions the order goes back to normal: 'Can you tell me where you are going?'

cards.title: Fix one mistake at a time
cards.body: Do not try to fix everything at once. Choose **one** mistake from this stage, for example 'since and for' or 'a/an before jobs', and listen for it for one week. Write three correct sentences about your own life each morning: 'I have lived in Faisalabad since 2015.' When it feels automatic, choose the next one.

cards.title: Take-aways from the Repair Workshop
items: Use 'have been doing' with since (a starting point) and for (a length of time).
Avoid -ing with state verbs: I have, I know, I understand, I want.
After did or didn't, use the base verb: 'Did you go?' 'I didn't see it.'
Use a or an by sound before jobs and single things; use the when both people know which one.
Say 'discuss the plan', 'return on Monday', 'married to', 'angry with' and 'at 5 p.m. on Monday'.
Keep v and w different, start s-clusters without an extra vowel, and stress the right part of the word.

cards.prompt: Record yourself reading the six correct sentences from 'Six grammar repairs' and the six words from 'Say it clearly'. Which one was hardest for you? Plan how you will practise it this week.

quiz.question: Which sentence uses 'since' and 'for' correctly?
options: I am studying English since six months.
I have been studying English for six months.
I have been studying English since six months.
I study English for six months now since.
quiz.explanation: 'For' goes with a length of time (six months) and the present perfect shows the action started in the past and is still going on. 'Since' needs a starting point, such as 'since March'.

quiz.question: Which sentence about family is correct?
options: I am having two brothers and a sister.
I have two brothers and a sister.
I am have two brothers and a sister.
I having two brothers and one sister.
quiz.explanation: 'Have' for owning or family is a state, so English uses the simple form. 'I'm having lunch' is fine because eating is an action.

quiz.question: Choose the correct question.
options: Did you sent the invoice yesterday?
Did you sending the invoice yesterday?
You did sent the invoice yesterday?
Did you send the invoice yesterday?
quiz.explanation: 'Did' already shows the past tense, so the main verb stays in its base form: send, not sent.

quiz.question: Which sentence uses the correct article?
options: She wants to be architect.
She wants to be a architect.
She wants to be an architect.
She wants to be the architect in general.
quiz.explanation: Jobs take 'a' or 'an', and 'architect' starts with a vowel sound, so it needs 'an'.

quiz.question: Which is correct: '___ hour', '___ university', '___ MBA'?
options: an hour, a university, an MBA
a hour, a university, a MBA
an hour, an university, an MBA
a hour, an university, a MBA
quiz.explanation: Choose by the first sound: 'hour' starts with a vowel sound (the h is silent), 'university' starts with a 'yoo' sound, and 'MBA' starts with an 'em' sound.

quiz.question: Which sentence about a meeting plan is correct?
options: Let's discuss about the delivery dates tomorrow.
Let's discuss on the delivery dates tomorrow.
Let's do discussion about the delivery dates tomorrow.
Let's discuss the delivery dates tomorrow.
quiz.explanation: 'Discuss' takes a direct object with no preposition. You can say 'talk about' or 'have a discussion about', but not 'discuss about'.

quiz.question: Which sentence uses at, on and in correctly?
options: The interview is on 10 a.m. in Tuesday at March.
The interview is in 10 a.m. at Tuesday on March.
The interview is at 10 a.m. on Tuesday in March.
The interview will be at 10 a.m. in Tuesday on March.
quiz.explanation: Use 'at' for exact times, 'on' for days and dates, and 'in' for months, years and seasons.

quiz.question: Bilal says 'vine' but his listener hears 'wine'. What should he practise?
options: Speaking much faster so the listener does not notice the sound
Adding a short vowel before the v sound to make it stronger
Using the same sound for both letters, as they mean the same
Touching his top teeth to his bottom lip for v, and rounding his lips with no teeth for w
quiz.explanation: English treats v and w as separate sounds that change meaning. The teeth-on-lip position makes v; rounded lips make w.

quiz.question: Which indirect question has the correct word order?
options: Could you tell me when the meeting starts?
Could you tell me when does the meeting start?
Could you tell me when starts the meeting?
Could you tell me when is the meeting starting?
quiz.explanation: After 'Could you tell me...', the question words go back to normal sentence order: subject, then verb. There is no 'does'.

quiz.question: Where is the stress in the word 'photography'?
options: On the second part: pho-TO-gra-phy
On the first part: PHO-to-gra-phy
On the last part: pho-to-gra-PHY
Evenly on every part, with no stress
quiz.explanation: 'Photograph' is stressed at the start, but 'photography' moves the stress to the second part. Getting stress right helps listeners recognise the word.

sessions.title: On the Line: Phone Calls and Polite Requests
sessions.summary: Answer and make work phone calls in English, ask people to repeat or spell, take and leave clear messages, read numbers so they are heard correctly, and make requests that sound polite rather than bossy.
objectives: Open, transfer and close a business phone call using standard phrases
Ask for repetition and spell names, e-mail addresses and codes clearly
Take and leave a complete phone message and confirm the details
Make polite requests with could, would and would you mind, and answer them correctly

cards.title: The phone that nobody wanted to answer
cards.setting: The sales office of a textile unit on Jhang Road, Faisalabad. Tuesday, 4:30 p.m.

lines.text: Bilal's manager is at the bank. The office phone rings. The screen shows a number from the United Kingdom.
(to himself) Not again. If I answer and don't understand, the buyer will think we are not professional.
(answering) Hello? Yes? ... Sorry? ... Okay, okay. Bye. (He hangs up.) I didn't catch her name, her company or what she wanted.
(on a video call that evening) Bilal, you did the brave part: you answered. Now we give you the tools for the rest.
Phone calls follow a pattern. Learn twenty phrases, practise asking people to repeat and spell, and you will never hang up empty-handed again.
And I'll be the buyer for practice. I can be very fast and very confusing!

cards.title: The shape of a business call

scenes.heading: Open clearly
scenes.narration: Say a greeting, the company name and your name: 'Good afternoon, Noor Textiles, Bilal speaking. How can I help you?' The caller knows at once they have the right place.

scenes.heading: Find out who and why
scenes.narration: 'May I ask who's calling?' 'And what is it regarding?' Write the name down straight away. If you miss it, ask again: it is normal and polite.

scenes.heading: Help, transfer or take a message
scenes.narration: If you can help, do. If not: 'One moment, please, I'll put you through.' or 'I'm afraid he's not available right now. Can I take a message?'

scenes.heading: Check the details
scenes.narration: Read back names, numbers and dates: 'Just to confirm, that's Ms Clarke, order 4471, delivery on 12 March. Is that right?'

scenes.heading: Close warmly
scenes.narration: 'Thank you for calling. I'll make sure he gets your message today. Have a good afternoon.' Let the caller hang up first if you can.

cards.title: Answering a business call
cards.caption: Five steps you can use for almost every incoming call.

items.label: Greet and name
items.detail: Greeting, company name, your name.

items.label: Ask who and why
items.detail: 'May I ask who's calling?' 'What is it regarding?'

items.label: Help or route
items.detail: Answer, transfer or offer to take a message.

items.label: Read back details
items.detail: Names, numbers, dates and the next step.

items.label: Close politely
items.detail: Thank them and say what will happen next.

cards.question: A caller speaks very fast and Bilal does not understand. What should he say?
options: 'Sorry, could you say that again a little more slowly, please?'
'What? Speak properly.'
'Yes, yes, okay.' and hope it was not important
'My English is very bad, please call tomorrow.'
cards.explanation: Asking someone to repeat more slowly is normal and polite in every country. Pretending to understand causes mistakes, and blaming your English ends the call without helping anyone.

cards.title: Phrases for when you didn't catch it

cards.back: 'Sorry, I didn't catch that. Could you repeat it, please?'
'Could you speak a little more slowly, please?'
'Sorry, the delivery date was... which day?'
'Could you spell that for me, please?'
'I'm sorry, the line is breaking up. Could I call you back?'
'Just to confirm, you said fifteen, one-five, not fifty?'

cards.title: Spelling and numbers that are heard correctly
cards.body:
On the phone, letters such as **b, d, p, t** and **m, n** sound alike. Use the international spelling alphabet: 'That's **C** for Charlie, **L** for Lima, **A** for Alpha, **R** for Romeo, **K** for Kilo, **E** for Echo: Clarke.'

**E-mail addresses:** say '@' as **at** and '.' as **dot**. 'bilal dot ahmed at noortextiles dot com'. Say whether there is an underscore or a hyphen (also called a dash).

**Phone numbers:** say them in small groups with short pauses: 'oh-three-oh-oh... one-two-three... four-five-six-seven'. Many British speakers say **double** for repeated digits ('double five'); many American speakers just repeat the digit.

**Teens and tens:** stress the end of fif-**TEEN** and the start of **FIF**-ty, and confirm big numbers digit by digit: 'fifteen, that's one-five.'

cards.title: Spell it like a professional
cards.prompt: Match each letter to its word in the international spelling alphabet.

cards.title: From bossy to polite
cards.caption: Each step down is softer. For most work requests, aim for the middle or lower steps.

items.label: Send me the file.
items.detail: An order. Fine in an emergency, but it sounds rude in most work requests.

items.label: Please send me the file.
items.detail: Still direct. 'Please' alone does not always soften an order.

items.label: Can you send me the file?
items.detail: Friendly and common between colleagues.

items.label: Could you send me the file?
items.detail: More polite. Good for clients and seniors.

items.label: Would you mind sending me the file?
items.detail: Very polite. Note the -ing form after 'mind'.

items.label: I was wondering if you could send me the file.
items.detail: Most tentative. Useful for a big favour or a busy senior.

cards.title: Too direct or polite?
cards.prompt: Sort each request you might make to a client or a senior colleague.

items.text: 'Send the payment today.'
'Tell me your order number.'
'Kindly revert immediately.'
'Give me a discount.'
'Could you confirm the payment date?'
'Would you mind checking the order number for me?'
'I was wondering if we could move the call to Thursday.'
'Could I ask a quick favour?'

cards.question: A client asks Bilal, 'Would you mind sending the samples by courier?' Bilal is happy to do it. What is the correct short reply?
options: 'No, not at all. I'll send them today.'
'Yes, I mind. I'll send them today.'
'Yes, I would mind.'
'I don't send them.'
cards.explanation: 'Would you mind...?' literally asks whether it bothers you. 'No, not at all' means 'It's no trouble, I'm happy to.' Saying 'Yes' would mean you object.

cards.title: Taking a message for the manager
cards.situation: A buyer, Ms Rebecca Clarke, calls from Leeds. She asks for Bilal's manager, who is out. She says she needs the revised price list for order 4471 before Thursday and wants a call back. She speaks quickly. What should Bilal do?

choices.text: Say his manager is out, offer to take a message, spell her name back, read back the order number and deadline, and confirm her phone number
choices.outcome: Ms Clarke says, 'Perfect, thank you, Bilal.' His note has her name, company, order number, deadline and number. His manager calls her back the same afternoon. Complete details turned a missed call into a sale on time.

choices.text: Say his manager is out and ask her to call back tomorrow
choices.outcome: Polite, but she now has to do the work again and may call another supplier. Offering to take a message keeps the customer and the order in your hands.

choices.text: Write 'Rebecca called, prices' on a scrap of paper and hang up quickly
choices.outcome: His manager has no surname, number, order or deadline. He has to search old e-mails to find her, and the price list is late. A rushed message is almost as bad as no message.

cards.title: Leave a voicemail that gets a call back
cards.prompt: Put the parts of a clear voicemail message into order.
steps: Greet and give your name and company
Say why you are calling in one sentence
Say what you need and by when
Give your number slowly, in groups, and repeat it

cards.title: Ayesha practises a full call
cards.body:
Sana listens as Ayesha calls a company about an internship.

**Receptionist:** 'Good morning, Bright Star Media.'
**Ayesha:** 'Good morning. My name is Ayesha Malik. Could I speak to someone in the HR team, please?'
**Receptionist:** 'May I ask what it's regarding?'
**Ayesha:** 'I'm calling about the internship advertised on your website. I wanted to check the closing date.'
**Receptionist:** 'It's the twentieth of this month.'
**Ayesha:** 'Just to confirm, the twentieth, two-zero? Thank you. And should I send my CV to the address on the website?'
**Receptionist:** 'Yes, that's right.'
**Ayesha:** 'Thank you for your help. Have a good day.'

Short, polite and every detail checked.

cards.title: Take-aways from the Call Desk
items: Open with a greeting, the company name and your name; close by saying what will happen next.
Asking someone to repeat, slow down or spell is normal and professional.
Use the spelling alphabet and say numbers in groups; confirm teens and tens digit by digit.
A complete message has the name, company, number, reason, deadline and next step.
Soften requests with could, would and would you mind + -ing; 'Not at all' means 'Happy to.'

cards.prompt: Think of a phone call you avoided or found difficult. Write the five phrases you would use if it happened again tomorrow, then say them aloud three times.

quiz.question: What is the best way to answer the office phone at work?
options: 'Hello? Who is this and what do you want from us?'
'Yes?'
'Good morning, Noor Textiles, Bilal speaking. How can I help you?'
'Hello, hello, hello, can you hear me now? Who is it?'
quiz.explanation: A greeting, the company name and your name tell the caller they have reached the right place and set a professional tone.

quiz.question: In the international spelling alphabet, how would you spell the name 'MIR'?
options: Mother, Indigo, Rose
Mango, Igloo, Robert
Mike, Ice, Rome
Mike, India, Romeo
quiz.explanation: The international spelling alphabet uses fixed words: M is Mike, I is India and R is Romeo. Using the standard words avoids confusion.

quiz.question: A customer says the amount is 'fifteen thousand'. What is the best way to confirm it?
options: 'Okay, fifty thousand. Thank you, I have written it down.'
'Sorry, numbers are hard on the phone, please e-mail.'
'Just to confirm, that's fifteen, one-five, thousand?'
'Fifteen or fifty, it's the same, I'll check later.'
quiz.explanation: Teens and tens sound alike on the phone. Reading back the digits removes doubt before money or stock is affected.

quiz.question: Which request is the most polite way to ask a senior manager for a favour?
options: 'Look at my report.'
'Please look at my report today, I need it urgently.'
'I was wondering if you could look at my report.'
'You will look at my report.'
quiz.explanation: 'I was wondering if you could...' is the most tentative and respectful of these. The others are orders, even with 'please'.

quiz.question: Which sentence is grammatically correct?
options: Would you mind calling me back after lunch?
Would you mind to call me back after lunch?
Would you mind call me back after lunch?
Would you mind if call me back after your lunch break?
quiz.explanation: 'Would you mind' is followed by the -ing form of the verb: 'mind calling', 'mind sending', 'mind checking'.

quiz.question: A client asks, 'Would you mind waiting a moment?' You are happy to wait. What do you say?
options: 'Yes, I would.'
'Not at all.'
'Yes, I mind.'
'I mind, but okay.'
quiz.explanation: The question asks whether waiting bothers you. 'Not at all' means it doesn't, so you are happy to wait.

quiz.question: How should you say the e-mail address ayesha.malik@brightstar.pk on the phone?
options: 'ayesha full stop malik at the rate brightstar full stop p-k'
'ayesha dot malik at brightstar dot p-k'
'ayesha point malik circle a brightstar point p-k'
'ayesha malik brightstar p-k' without the symbols
quiz.explanation: In e-mail addresses, '.' is said as 'dot' and '@' as 'at'. 'At the rate' is used in parts of South Asia but can confuse international listeners.

quiz.question: Which detail is most often missing from a weak phone message?
options: The colour of the caller's company logo
Whether the caller had a nice voice
The weather in the caller's city that day
The caller's number and the deadline for the call back
quiz.explanation: A useful message has the caller's name, company, number, reason, deadline and next step. Without a number and deadline, nobody can act on it.

quiz.question: The line is bad and you can only hear half of what the caller says. What is the best response?
options: Keep saying 'yes' and hope the call improves
'I'm sorry, the line is breaking up. Could I call you back on this number?'
Hang up without saying anything and wait for them to call again
Shout louder so they can hear you better
quiz.explanation: Naming the problem and offering to call back is polite and solves it. Pretending to hear causes mistakes, and hanging up silently looks rude.

quiz.question: Why does 'Please send me the file' sometimes still sound bossy?
options: Because 'file' is an informal word that should never be used in any office
Because English never uses 'please' in business
Because requests must always be written, never spoken
It is still an order; 'please' alone does not always make it a request
quiz.explanation: In English, a question such as 'Could you send me the file?' sounds more like a request than an order with 'please' added. Both are understood, but the question form is softer.

sessions.title: Speaking Up in Meetings and Job Interviews
sessions.summary: Move from everyday English to job-ready English: give opinions, agree, disagree and interrupt politely in meetings, then answer interview questions with a strong self-introduction and well-structured STAR stories.
objectives: Use meeting phrases to give opinions, agree, disagree, interrupt and clarify politely
Avoid common meeting mistakes such as 'I am agree' and 'I didn't get you'
Answer 'Tell me about yourself' with a focused 60 to 90 second answer
Structure behavioural interview answers with the STAR method in the past tense
Handle difficult interview moments: unclear questions, weaknesses and your own questions at the end

cards.title: Two big days in one week
cards.setting: The Speaking Circle, Gulberg, Lahore. Thursday evening, one month after the first meeting.

lines.text: I got the call! A software house in Johar Town wants to interview me on Monday for a digital marketing executive role.
And my internship interview with a Karachi bank is on Wednesday. It's online. Last time, they asked 'Tell me about yourself' and I talked for five minutes about my school.
My problem is meetings. Our new export manager runs them in English. I have good ideas, but by the time I prepare my sentence, the topic has changed.
Welcome to the Premium stages. Until now, we built confidence. Now we build job-ready English: the phrases and structures that interviewers and managers listen for.
Tonight: meeting phrases for Bilal, and two interview tools for Ayesha and Hamza. A 90-second introduction, and the STAR method for every 'Tell me about a time...' question.

cards.title: Meeting phrases by purpose
cards.caption: Have one ready phrase in each box. Then you can join the conversation without building a sentence from nothing.

items.label: Giving an opinion
items.detail: 'In my view, we should...' 'I think the main issue is...'

items.label: Agreeing
items.detail: 'I agree with Sara on that.' 'That's a good point.'

items.label: Disagreeing politely
items.detail: 'I see your point, but...' 'I'm not sure that will work, because...'

items.label: Clarifying
items.detail: 'Sorry, could you explain what you mean by...?' 'So, are you saying...?'

cards.back: 'I agree with you.' Agree is a verb, so it does not need 'am'.
Understood locally, but clearer as: 'Sorry, I didn't quite follow. Could you explain that again?'
'What should we do next?'
'I don't think that's right.' Focus on the idea, not the person.
'Can I ask a question?' or 'I have a quick question.'
'Could I just finish my point?'

scenes.heading: Interrupt politely
scenes.narration: Wait for a small pause, then: 'Sorry to interrupt, could I just add something?' Short and polite, and it works in nearly every meeting.

scenes.heading: Hold your turn
scenes.narration: If someone talks over you: 'Could I just finish my point? Then I'd love to hear yours.' Calm, not angry.

scenes.heading: Check before you argue
scenes.narration: Many disagreements are misunderstandings. 'So, if I understand correctly, you want to launch in March, not April?'

scenes.heading: Disagree with the idea, not the person
scenes.narration: 'I see why you suggest that. My concern is the cost.' Name the concern and, if you can, offer another option.

scenes.heading: Sum up at the end
scenes.narration: 'So, to sum up, we've agreed that Bilal will send the samples by Friday.' Whoever summarises often looks like the most organised person in the room.

cards.question: In a meeting, the export manager suggests sending all samples by air. Bilal thinks sea freight is cheaper and fast enough. Which response is best?
options: 'That is wrong. Air is a waste of money.'
Stay silent, because disagreeing with a manager is impolite
'I see the benefit of air, but sea freight would save cost and still arrive in time. Could we compare both?'
'I am disagree with you, sir.'
cards.explanation: Acknowledging the idea, giving a reason and suggesting a next step is polite and persuasive. Silence loses the idea, and 'I am disagree' is a grammar mistake: say 'I disagree'.

cards.title: 'Tell me about yourself': a 90-second answer
cards.body:
This is often the first question, and it sets the tone for the whole interview. The interviewer does not want your life story. They want to know: **who are you, and why are you right for this job?**

Use the **present, past, future** shape from Stage 1, but focus it on the job:

- **Present (15 seconds):** what you do or study now. 'I'm a business graduate who loves digital marketing.'
- **Past (45 seconds):** two or three experiences that match the job. 'In my internship I ran social media posts for a savings campaign...'
- **Future (20 seconds):** why this role. 'I'm excited about this role because your company builds apps for small businesses, and I want to market products that help people.'

Keep it between 60 and 90 seconds. Practise it aloud, but **do not memorise it word for word**: learn the three parts and a few key phrases, so it sounds natural.

cards.title: The STAR method
cards.caption: Use it for any question that starts 'Tell me about a time when...' or 'Give an example of...'.

items.label: Situation
items.detail: Set the scene briefly: where, when, what was happening. One or two sentences.

items.label: Task
items.detail: Your responsibility or the problem you had to solve.

items.label: Action
items.detail: What you did, step by step. Use 'I', not only 'we'. This is the longest part.

items.label: Result
items.detail: What happened, and what you learned. Give a clear outcome, and numbers only if they are true.

cards.title: Ayesha's STAR answer
cards.body:
**Question:** 'Tell me about a time you improved something.'

**Situation:** 'During my internship at a bank in Lahore, our Facebook posts for a savings account were getting very few comments.'

**Task:** 'My supervisor asked me to make the posts more engaging over six weeks.'

**Action:** 'First, I asked twenty customers in the branch what they wanted to know. Then I made short videos in simple Urdu and English that answered their top three questions. I also posted in the evening, when our page was busiest, and I replied to every comment within a day.'

**Result:** 'By the end, comments and shares were about double the previous campaign, and my supervisor used the video format for the next product. I learned to start with the customer's questions, not with our message.'

Notice: **past tense**, **'I' for her own actions**, and a result she can honestly explain.

cards.title: Build Hamza's STAR answer
cards.prompt: Hamza is asked, 'Tell me about a time you worked in a team.' Put his answer into STAR order.
steps: 'In my third year, four of us had to build a library app for our final project.'
'I was responsible for the database and for keeping the team on schedule.'
'I made a shared task list, set a short call every Sunday and helped a teammate who was stuck on the login page.'
'We submitted a week early and got an A. I learned that a simple weekly check-in prevents most problems.'

cards.title: Strong or weak interview answer?
cards.prompt: Sort each answer an interviewer might hear.

items.text: 'I organised a fundraiser at my university. I contacted ten local shops for prizes and we raised enough for two scholarships.'
'My weakness is public speaking, so I joined an English speaking club and I now present every week.'
'Could you repeat the question, please? I want to make sure I answer it properly.'
'What does a typical week look like for someone in this role?'
'I am a hard worker, honest, punctual and I work well in a team.' (with no examples)
'My weakness is that I am a perfectionist and I work too hard.'
'We did everything as a team, so I can't say what I did myself.'
'No, I don't have any questions.'

cards.title: An unclear question in the online interview
cards.situation: In his online interview, Hamza hears: 'How would you prioritise competing stakeholder requirements in a sprint?' He knows what a sprint is from his project, but he is not sure what 'competing stakeholder requirements' means here. The interviewer is waiting. What should he do?

choices.text: Say: 'That's a good question. Just to check I understand: do you mean when different people want different things from the team at the same time?' Then answer with an example.
choices.outcome: The interviewer says, 'Exactly.' Hamza gives a short STAR example from his project. Checking the question showed calm thinking and good communication, which is exactly what interviewers want to see.

choices.text: Say: 'Could you repeat the question, please?' and then answer as best he can
choices.outcome: Repeating helps if he missed words, but the problem was meaning, not sound. Hearing it again, he is still not sure. Rephrasing the question in his own words would have been more useful.

choices.text: Start talking straight away about anything related to sprints so there is no silence
choices.outcome: He talks for two minutes without answering the question. A short pause or a clarifying question is much better than a long answer to the wrong question.

cards.question: Which answer to 'What is your biggest weakness?' is strongest?
options: 'I used to avoid speaking up in meetings, so I joined a speaking club and now I share one idea in every meeting.'
'I don't have any weaknesses that would affect my work in this role.'
'I am a perfectionist and I work too hard.'
'I am always late, but I am trying.'
cards.explanation: A strong answer names a real but manageable weakness and shows what you are doing about it. 'No weaknesses' and the 'perfectionist' cliche sound unprepared, and lateness is a serious problem for most employers.

cards.title: Interview English habits
cards.body:
- **Use the past tense for stories:** 'I organised', 'I contacted', 'we finished'.
- **Pause instead of filling silence:** 'Let me think for a moment.' is better than 'umm... basically... actually...'.
- **Ask two questions at the end:** 'What would success look like in the first three months?' 'What do you enjoy most about working here?'
- **Online:** test your camera and microphone, sit in a quiet room with light in front of you, and look at the camera when you speak.
- **Never make up results.** Interviewers often ask follow-up questions.

cards.title: Take-aways from the Interview Room
items: Keep one ready phrase for opinions, agreeing, disagreeing and clarifying in meetings.
Say 'I agree' and 'I disagree', not 'I am agree'. Disagree with the idea, not the person.
Interrupt with 'Sorry to interrupt...' and hold your turn with 'Could I just finish my point?'
Answer 'Tell me about yourself' in 60 to 90 seconds: present, past, future, linked to the job.
Use STAR for 'Tell me about a time...' questions, with the past tense and 'I' for your actions.
Clarify unclear questions, give an honest weakness with an action, and ask questions at the end.

cards.prompt: Write your own 90-second 'Tell me about yourself' answer and one STAR story from your studies or work. Record both, listen back and check: is the past tense correct, and did you say what you did?

quiz.question: Which sentence is correct in a meeting?
options: 'I am agree with Bilal about the delivery date.'
'I agree with Bilal about the delivery date.'
'I am agreeing to Bilal on the delivery date.'
'I agreed with Bilal on the delivery date now.'
quiz.explanation: 'Agree' is a verb, so it does not need 'am'. Say 'I agree' and 'I disagree'.

quiz.question: Bilal wants to add a point while his manager is speaking. What is the best phrase?
options: Start talking louder than the manager until everyone listens to him instead
Say 'Stop, stop, listen to me first' immediately
Wait until after the meeting and tell a colleague instead
Wait for a pause, then: 'Sorry to interrupt, could I just add something?'
quiz.explanation: A short apology and a request let you join the conversation politely. Shouting over people is rude, and waiting until after the meeting means the idea is lost.

quiz.question: What is the best length for an answer to 'Tell me about yourself' in an interview?
options: About 60 to 90 seconds
About five to ten minutes, covering your whole education and family
One sentence of fewer than ten words
As long as it takes to read your full CV aloud
quiz.explanation: 60 to 90 seconds is long enough to show who you are and why you fit the job, and short enough to keep the interviewer interested.

quiz.question: In the STAR method, what does the 'T' stand for?
options: Task: your responsibility or the problem you had to solve
Team: a list of everyone who worked with you on the project
Time: the exact date and hour the story happened
Talent: the skill you are most proud of in yourself
quiz.explanation: STAR stands for Situation, Task, Action and Result. The task is what you were responsible for in that situation.

quiz.question: Which part of a STAR answer should usually be the longest?
options: Situation: all the background about the company and the people
Task: a full description of the job you had at that time
Action: what you did, step by step
Result: a long list of every number you can remember
quiz.explanation: Interviewers most want to know what you did and how you thought. Keep the situation short and spend most time on your actions.

quiz.question: Hamza says, 'We made a plan and we finished early.' Why might an interviewer ask a follow-up question?
options: Because using the past tense in an interview is a grammar mistake
Because teamwork examples are not allowed in interviews
They cannot tell what Hamza himself did
Because 'finished early' sounds like he did not work hard
quiz.explanation: Teamwork is good, but in STAR answers the interviewer is assessing you. Use 'I' for your own actions, such as 'I made the task list'.

quiz.question: Which is the best way to disagree politely with a colleague's idea?
options: 'You are wrong, and that idea will never work.'
'I see your point, but I'm worried about the cost. Could we look at another option?'
'He is telling wrong.'
'Fine, do what you want.'
quiz.explanation: Acknowledge the idea, give your concern and suggest a next step. This keeps the focus on the idea, not on the person.

quiz.question: During an interview, you don't understand what a question means. What is the best response?
options: Answer a different question that you prepared before the interview
Say nothing and wait for them to ask the next question
Rephrase it to check: 'Just to check, do you mean...?'
Say 'I didn't get you' and stop there
quiz.explanation: Checking the meaning in your own words shows calm, careful communication. Then you can give a focused answer.

quiz.question: Which question is a strong one to ask at the end of an interview?
options: 'How many days off do I get, and can I leave early every Friday?'
'No, I don't have any questions. Thank you.'
'What would success look like in this role after three months?'
'What does your company do?'
quiz.explanation: A question about success in the role shows interest and planning. Asking what the company does shows you did not prepare.

quiz.question: Which sentence would be the best way to close a meeting?
options: 'Okay, that's all, bye everyone.'
'So, to sum up, Ayesha will send the draft by Thursday and we'll review it on Friday.'
'What to do now?'
'We discussed many things today, thank you for coming.'
quiz.explanation: A short summary of who will do what and by when makes sure everyone leaves with the same understanding.

sessions.title: Presentations and Persuasive Speaking in English
sessions.summary: Give presentations in English that are easy to follow and hard to forget: signposting phrases, describing numbers and trends correctly, using your voice to stress key words, persuasive language that stays honest, and calm English for questions.
objectives: Use signposting phrases to open, move between points and close a presentation
Describe numbers and trends correctly with rise, fall, by, to and adverbs such as sharply and slightly
Use stress, pauses and short sentences so key points land
Build a persuasive case with problem, solution and benefit, and confident but honest language
Handle questions in English, including ones you cannot answer straight away

cards.title: Ten minutes to win a buyer
cards.setting: The meeting room of a textile unit in Faisalabad. Monday, 11 a.m. A buyer delegation from abroad arrives on Wednesday.

lines.text: My manager wants me to present our new range of cotton bedsheets to the buyers. Ten minutes, in English. I have the slides. I don't have the words.
Show me what you planned to say for the sales slide.
'This is the graph. The sales are going up and down and then they are increasing very much.'
I have the same problem with my class presentation. My slides are good, but I just read them out.
Your content is strong. What you need is the language that guides listeners: where you are going, what the numbers mean, and why they should say yes.
By Wednesday, Bilal, you'll describe that graph in one clear sentence, and the buyers will remember your main point.

cards.title: Signposts: telling the audience where you are

scenes.heading: Open and give a map
scenes.narration: 'Good morning, everyone. Thank you for coming. Today I'd like to show you our new bedsheet range. I'll cover three things: the product, the numbers and the next steps.'

scenes.heading: Move between points
scenes.narration: 'That's the product. Now let's move on to the numbers.' 'This brings me to my last point.' Each signpost tells listeners a new section has started.

scenes.heading: Point to visuals
scenes.narration: 'As you can see on this slide...' 'If you look at the blue line...' Then stop and give people a moment to look.

scenes.heading: Sum up
scenes.narration: 'So, to sum up: high-quality cotton, steady demand and delivery in six weeks.' Repeat your main message in one sentence.

scenes.heading: Invite questions
scenes.narration: 'Thank you. I'm happy to take any questions.' Not just 'That's all' or 'Finished.'

cards.title: Signpost for every moment
cards.prompt: Match each moment in a presentation with a phrase that fits.

pairs.right: 'Today I'd like to talk about three things.'
'To give you an example, last month a shop in Lahore ordered...'
'As you can see from this chart...'
'To sum up, the main point is...'

cards.title: Words for trends
cards.caption: Choose the verb for the direction and the adverb for the speed or size.

items.label: No change
items.left: remain steady, stay the same, level off

cards.title: By or to? Small words, big difference
cards.body:
In trend sentences, two small prepositions change the meaning completely.

- **by** = the amount of change. 'Sales rose **by** 500 units.' (They are now 500 units higher.)
- **to** = the new level. 'Sales rose **to** 5,000 units.'
- **from... to...** = start and end. 'Sales rose **from** 4,000 **to** 5,000 units.'

**Tense matters too.** Use the past simple for a finished period: 'Orders **increased** last year.' Use the present perfect for a change up to now: 'Orders **have increased** since January.'

Bilal's new sentence: 'As you can see, orders **rose steadily from** 3,000 **to** 5,000 sets between January and June.' One clear sentence, one clear message. (These are the fictional numbers on Bilal's slide; always use your own real figures.)

cards.question: Bilal's chart shows orders went from 2,000 to 2,500. Which sentence is correct?
options: 'Orders rose to 500 by 2,500.'
'Orders rose by 500 to 2,500.'
'Orders rose by 2,500 to 500.'
'Orders are rising by 500 to 2,500 last month.'
cards.explanation: 'By' gives the size of the change (500) and 'to' gives the new level (2,500). The last option also mixes a present continuous verb with 'last month'.

cards.title: Your voice does half the work

scenes.heading: Stress the key word
scenes.narration: In 'We deliver in SIX weeks, not ten', the stressed word carries the message. Choose one key word in each important sentence and say it a little louder and longer.

scenes.heading: Pause after big points
scenes.narration: After your main point, stop for two seconds. Silence tells listeners: this matters. It also gives you time to breathe.

scenes.heading: Short sentences
scenes.narration: Long sentences are hard to say and hard to follow. One idea per sentence. 'Our cotton is soft. It lasts. And it arrives on time.'

scenes.heading: Slow down for numbers
scenes.narration: Say numbers slowly and repeat the important ones: 'Six weeks. Six weeks from order to your warehouse.'

cards.title: Problem, solution, benefit
cards.caption: A simple persuasive structure for a pitch, a proposal or a request to your manager.

items.label: Problem
items.detail: What the listener is struggling with: 'Your customers want softer sheets at a fair price.'

items.label: Solution
items.detail: What you offer: 'Our new range uses long-staple cotton and a tighter weave.'

items.label: Proof
items.detail: Why they should believe you: samples, a test, a customer they can call.

items.label: Benefit
items.detail: What they gain, in their words: 'Fewer returns and repeat customers.'

items.label: Call to action
items.detail: One clear next step: 'I'd like to send you fifty sample sets this week.'

cards.back: Use 'you' and 'your customers' more than 'we' and 'our company'.
Group ideas in threes: 'soft, strong and on time'. Three is easy to remember.
'Not the cheapest, but the best value over a year.'
'What does a late delivery cost you in December?' Then pause.
'I recommend...' instead of 'Maybe we can perhaps think about...'
Say 'in our tests' or 'our customers tell us'. Never invent numbers or promises you cannot keep.

cards.title: Confident or weak?
cards.prompt: Sort each sentence from a presentation.

items.text: 'I recommend we start with a trial order of fifty sets.'
'Our sheets are soft, strong and delivered on time.'
'As you can see, returns fell by half after we changed the stitching.'
'What would fewer returns mean for your business?'
'So basically, actually, this is the graph, I think.'
'Maybe, if possible, perhaps you could consider maybe ordering.'
'The sales are going up and down and then increasing very much.'
'That's all. Finished.'

cards.question: Which ending is strongest for Bilal's ten-minute presentation?
options: 'To sum up: soft, strong, on time. I'd like to send you fifty sample sets this week. I'm happy to take any questions.'
'Okay, that's all from my side, thank you very much.'
'So that was the presentation about the product and the numbers.'
'Any questions? No? Okay, finished.'
cards.explanation: A strong close repeats the main message, makes one clear request and invites questions. The other endings give the audience nothing to remember or act on.

cards.title: A question Bilal can't answer
cards.situation: At the end of his talk, a buyer asks: 'What is the shrinkage rate after five washes at 60 degrees?' Bilal does not know the exact figure. The quality team tested it, but he did not bring the report. Everyone is looking at him. What should he say?

choices.text: 'That's an important question. I don't have the exact test figure with me, and I don't want to guess. I'll e-mail you the quality report by tomorrow afternoon.'
choices.outcome: The buyer nods and writes it down. Bilal sends the report the next day. Admitting he did not have the figure, and promising a specific time, made him look honest and reliable.

choices.text: 'Shrinkage is very low, almost zero. Don't worry about it.'
choices.outcome: The buyer's own test later shows a different figure, and trust is damaged. Guessing in a sales presentation is a serious risk. Never invent a number.

choices.text: 'Sorry, I don't know.' and move to the next question
choices.outcome: It is honest, but it leaves the buyer without an answer. Adding 'I'll find out and send it to you by...' turns 'I don't know' into a professional promise.

cards.title: Q&A phrases to keep ready
cards.body:
- **To buy a second to think:** 'Thank you for the question.' (Use it once or twice, not before every answer.)
- **To check:** 'If I understand correctly, you're asking about...'
- **When you don't know:** 'I don't have that figure with me. I'll send it to you by...'
- **Off topic:** 'That's a little outside today's topic, but I'm happy to talk about it afterwards.'
- **To finish:** 'Does that answer your question?'

cards.title: Take-aways from the Main Stage
items: Signpost every section: give a map, move on clearly, sum up and invite questions.
Describe trends with a direction verb and an adverb: 'rose sharply', 'fell slightly', 'remained steady'.
Use 'by' for the amount of change and 'to' for the new level.
Stress one key word, pause after big points and slow down for numbers.
Persuade with problem, solution, proof, benefit and one clear call to action.
Be honest: never guess a figure. Promise to send it by a specific time.

cards.prompt: Choose a chart from your studies or work. Write one sentence that describes its main trend with a verb, an adverb and 'from... to...'. Then say it aloud, stressing the key word and pausing after it.

quiz.question: Which phrase is the best way to move to the next section of a presentation?
options: 'Next slide, next slide, okay, this one.'
'Now let's move on to the costs.'
'And also another thing is there.'
'So basically now the costs thing.'
quiz.explanation: A clear signpost tells listeners one section has ended and a new one has started, so they can follow your structure.

quiz.question: Sales went from 400 to 600 units. Which sentence is correct?
options: 'Sales rose by 400 units to 600 units.'
'Sales rose to 400 by 600 units.'
'Sales rose from 600 to 400 units.'
'Sales rose from 400 to 600 units.'
quiz.explanation: 'From... to...' gives the start and end levels. 'By' would give the size of the change, which here is 200, not 400.

quiz.question: Which sentence describes a small, slow change?
options: 'Costs increased sharply within a single month.'
'Costs increased gradually over the year.'
'Costs peaked in December.'
'Costs remained steady all year.'
quiz.explanation: 'Gradually' describes slow, steady change. 'Sharply' means fast and large, 'peaked' means reached the highest point and 'remained steady' means no change.

quiz.question: Which sentence uses the tense correctly?
options: 'Orders have increased last year.'
'Orders are increasing since January.'
'Orders have increased since January.'
'Orders increase since last January, every month.'
quiz.explanation: Use the present perfect with 'since' for a change up to now. A finished time such as 'last year' needs the past simple: 'Orders increased last year.'

quiz.question: What does pausing for two seconds after your main point do?
options: It shows the audience that you have forgotten what you had planned to say next
It wastes time that you should use for more slides
It signals that the point matters and gives listeners time to take it in
It is only useful in very large rooms with poor microphones
quiz.explanation: A deliberate pause highlights the point and lets it land. It also gives the speaker time to breathe and think.

quiz.question: In the problem-solution-benefit structure, what does the 'benefit' describe?
options: The technical features of your product, listed one by one
The history of your company since it was founded
The difficulties your own team had while making the product
What the listener gains, in their own terms
quiz.explanation: Benefits describe what the listener gets, such as fewer returns or happier customers. Features describe the product itself.

quiz.question: Which sentence sounds most confident without overclaiming?
options: 'I recommend a trial order, so you can test the quality yourself.'
'Maybe, if you want, perhaps we can think about a small order.'
'Our product is the best in the world and it will double your sales.'
'Please order, please, we really need this order.'
quiz.explanation: It is clear and confident, and the claim is honest. The second option makes promises nobody can guarantee, and the others sound weak or desperate.

quiz.question: A buyer asks for a figure you don't have with you. What is the most professional answer?
options: Give an approximate number that sounds about right, so that you don't lose the sale today
'That is not important, let's talk about something else.'
'I don't have that figure with me. I'll e-mail it to you by tomorrow afternoon.'
Pretend you didn't hear the question and move on to the next one
quiz.explanation: Honesty plus a specific promise builds trust. Guessing a figure can damage trust badly if it turns out to be wrong.

quiz.question: Which ending best closes a presentation?
options: 'To sum up, soft, strong and on time. I'm happy to take any questions.'
'Okay, finished.'
'That's all from my side, I think.'
'So that was everything I had, thank you, bye.'
quiz.explanation: A good close repeats the main message in a memorable way and invites questions, instead of just stopping.

quiz.question: Which technique is the 'rule of three'?
options: Showing exactly three slides in every presentation
Repeating every sentence three times so that nobody in the room misses it
Taking only three questions from the audience
Grouping ideas in threes, such as 'soft, strong and on time'
quiz.explanation: Three items are easy to say and easy to remember, so speakers often group key ideas in threes.

sessions.title: Professional Writing and Difficult Conversations
sessions.summary: Write e-mails that are clear, polite and understood by international readers, swap local phrases that confuse others, and find the right English words to give and receive feedback, say no, apologise and negotiate politely.
objectives: Structure a work e-mail with a clear subject line, purpose, request and close
Replace phrases such as 'do the needful', 'revert' and 'prepone' with internationally clear English
Give and receive feedback using specific, softened language
Say no, apologise and raise a problem politely using I-statements
Negotiate politely with conditionals, tentative language and a shared goal

cards.title: The e-mail that started an argument
cards.setting: A co-working space in Blue Area, Islamabad, where Ayesha now works as a digital marketing executive. Friday, 3 p.m.

lines.text: I wrote to a client in Dubai: 'Kindly do the needful and revert ASAP. PFA the file.' She replied: 'Sorry, what exactly do you need from me?'
Those phrases are common in offices here, but many international readers don't use them. 'Do the needful' doesn't say what you need, and 'revert' often means 'go back to an earlier state'.
And I have a different problem. A buyer wants a twenty per cent discount. I just wrote, 'Not possible.' Now he's gone quiet.
My team lead gave me feedback on my report and I said 'Sorry, sorry, sorry' five times. I didn't even ask what to change.
Then this is our last stage: the diplomat's desk. The words that let you say difficult things clearly and kindly, in writing and face to face.

cards.title: The shape of a clear work e-mail
cards.caption: Short, polite and easy to act on.

items.label: Subject line
items.detail: Specific: 'Revised price list for order 4471, needed by Thursday'.

items.label: Greeting
items.detail: 'Dear Ms Clarke,' for formal; 'Hi Sara,' for colleagues you know.

items.label: Purpose first
items.detail: 'I'm writing to ask for...' in the first sentence.

items.label: Details
items.detail: Short paragraphs or a short list: what, how many, when.

items.label: Clear request
items.detail: 'Could you send me the signed form by Wednesday?'

items.label: Close
items.detail: 'Thank you for your help. Kind regards, Ayesha'.

cards.title: Local phrases and clearer choices
cards.caption: These are understood in Pakistan, but they can confuse readers from other countries.

items.label: Do the needful
items.right: Could you please sign and return the form by Friday?

items.label: Prepone
items.right: Can we bring the meeting forward to 10 a.m.?

items.label: ASAP
items.right: Could you send it by 3 p.m. today? We need it for the client call.

cards.question: Ayesha needs a client to approve a design. Which sentence is clearest?
options: 'Could you approve the attached design by Wednesday, so we can print on Thursday?'
'Kindly do the needful regarding the design at the earliest.'
'PLEASE APPROVE THE DESIGN.'
'Please revert on the design.'
cards.explanation: It says exactly what to do, by when and why. 'Do the needful' and 'revert' are vague for many readers, and capital letters read as shouting.

scenes.heading: Softeners
scenes.narration: Words such as 'I'm afraid', 'unfortunately' and 'it seems' make bad news easier to hear: 'I'm afraid the shipment will be two days late.' The message is still clear.

scenes.heading: Past forms are softer
scenes.narration: 'I was wondering if...' and 'I wanted to ask...' sound more polite than 'I wonder' or 'I want'.

scenes.heading: Questions instead of orders
scenes.narration: 'Would it be possible to move the call?' is softer than 'Move the call.'

scenes.heading: But stay clear
scenes.narration: Too much softening hides the message. 'Maybe, if possible, perhaps...' leaves the reader unsure. One softener per sentence is usually enough.

cards.title: Giving and receiving feedback
cards.prompt: Match each situation with useful English for it.

pairs.left: Start with something specific and true
pairs.right: 'I liked how you opened the report with the key numbers.'
'One thing that could make it even stronger is a short summary at the top.'

pairs.left: Describe what you saw, not the person
pairs.right: 'I noticed the last two reports arrived after the deadline.'
'Thank you for telling me. Could you give me an example?'
'That makes sense. I'll add a summary from next week.'

cards.title: Saying no, apologising and raising a problem
cards.body:
These are the hardest things to say in any language. Short patterns help.

**Saying no politely:** say what you can't do, why, and what you can offer. 'I'd like to help, but I can't take this on before Friday because of the client launch. **Could** I start on Monday, or could Hamza help?'

**Apologising properly:** own it, fix it, prevent it. 'I'm sorry, I sent the wrong file. **Here is** the correct version, and I'll double-check attachments from now on.' One clear apology is better than 'sorry' five times.

**Raising a problem:** use an **I-statement**. 'I'm worried about the deadline, because the data arrived late twice this month. Can we agree a cut-off date?' This sounds very different from 'You are always late.'

cards.title: Polite and clear, or likely to cause trouble?
cards.prompt: Sort each sentence a colleague might write or say.

items.text: 'I'm afraid we can't deliver by Monday, but we can deliver on Wednesday.'
'I'm worried we'll miss the deadline. Can we talk about it today?'
'I'm sorry for the mistake. I've corrected the invoice and attached it.'
'Thanks for the feedback. Could you show me which part was unclear?'
'You never send anything on time.'
'Not possible.'
'THIS IS URGENT. REPLY NOW.'
'Sorry sorry sorry, my fault, sorry.'

cards.title: A polite negotiation
cards.caption: Keep returning to the shared goal until both sides can agree.

items.label: Shared goal
items.detail: 'We both want a long-term partnership that works for your shops.'

items.label: Ask and listen
items.detail: 'What matters most to you: price, speed or payment terms?'

items.label: Propose with if
