items.detail: 'If you order 500 sets, we can offer a five per cent discount.'

items.label: Respond softly
items.detail: 'That's a little higher than we can manage. What if we...?'

items.label: Confirm in writing
items.detail: 'Just to confirm what we agreed today...' by e-mail.

cards.back: 'That's a bit higher than our budget. Is there any flexibility?'
'If you can confirm by Friday, we can include free delivery.'
'Would you be able to extend the payment to 60 days?'
'Let me check with my manager and get back to you by tomorrow.'
'What if we split the order into two deliveries?'
'So, we've agreed on 500 sets with free delivery. I'll send a written summary today.'

cards.title: Bilal replies about the discount
cards.situation: A buyer has asked for a twenty per cent discount on an order of 300 sets. Bilal's manager has said the most they can offer is five per cent, and only for 500 sets or more. Bilal's first reply was 'Not possible.' The buyer has gone quiet. What should Bilal write now?

choices.text: 'Thank you for your patience. I'm afraid twenty per cent isn't possible on 300 sets. However, if you order 500 sets, we can offer a five per cent discount. Would that work for you?'
choices.outcome: The buyer replies the next morning to ask about delivery dates for 500 sets. Bilal said no clearly, gave a reason, and offered a real option with 'if'. The conversation is open again.

choices.text: 'Okay, fine, we can give twenty per cent.'
choices.outcome: Bilal has promised a discount his manager did not approve. The company loses money or Bilal has to take back his promise, which damages trust. Never agree to terms you are not allowed to give.

choices.text: 'Sorry for my earlier message. Please tell us what you think is fair.'
choices.outcome: The tone is warmer, but Bilal gives no offer and no limits. The buyer may simply repeat twenty per cent. A conditional offer moves the negotiation forward.

cards.question: Hamza's team lead says his report was too long. Which reply is best?
options: 'Sorry, sorry. I'm very sorry. Sorry.'
'Other people's reports are longer than mine.'
'Okay.' and make no changes
'Thanks for telling me. Which sections would you cut first?'
cards.explanation: Thanking the person and asking a specific question shows you take feedback seriously and want to improve. Repeated apologies and defensiveness do not help anyone fix the report.

cards.title: Read it aloud before you send
cards.body:
Before you send an important e-mail, read it aloud once.

- Would you say it this way to the person's face?
- Does the first sentence say why you are writing?
- Is your request clear, with a date?
- Have you removed 'do the needful', 'revert', 'PFA' and capital letters?

If the message is emotional, save it as a draft and read it again after an hour.

cards.title: Take-aways from the Diplomat's Desk
items: Clear e-mails have a specific subject line, purpose first, a clear request with a date and a polite close.
Swap 'do the needful', 'revert', 'prepone' and 'PFA' for plain, specific English.
Soften bad news with 'I'm afraid' or 'unfortunately', but keep the message clear.
Give feedback on what you saw, with a specific suggestion; receive it with thanks and a question.
Say no with a reason and an alternative; apologise once, fix it and say how you'll prevent it.
Negotiate with a shared goal, 'if' offers, soft responses and a written summary.

cards.prompt: Find an e-mail you sent recently. Rewrite it with a specific subject line, the purpose in the first sentence and a clear request with a date. What did you remove, and how does it sound now?

quiz.question: Which subject line is best for an e-mail asking a supplier for a corrected invoice?
options: 'Corrected invoice for order 2210 needed by Friday'
'Invoice'
'URGENT!!! PLEASE READ NOW'
'Hello, a small request from our side regarding something'
quiz.explanation: A specific subject line tells the reader what the e-mail is about and when action is needed, before they even open it.

quiz.question: What is a clearer way to write 'Please revert at the earliest'?
options: 'Please go back to the earliest version.'
'Could you reply by Tuesday?'
'Revert me fast, kindly.'
'Please do the needful at the earliest.'
quiz.explanation: Many international readers understand 'revert' as 'go back to an earlier state'. 'Reply' plus a specific day is clear to everyone.

quiz.question: A colleague abroad does not understand 'Can we prepone the meeting?' What should you write instead?
options: 'Can we bring the meeting forward to 10 a.m.?'
'Can we postpone the meeting to an earlier time?'
'Can we pre-move the meeting?'
'Can we do the meeting before?'
quiz.explanation: 'Prepone' is used in South Asia but not widely elsewhere. 'Bring forward' or 'move earlier' is understood everywhere. 'Postpone' means move later, so it would cause confusion.

quiz.question: Which sentence gives feedback on behaviour rather than on the person?
options: 'You are a very careless and lazy person.'
'You never care about deadlines.'
'Everyone says you are always late with reports.'
'I noticed the last two reports arrived after the deadline.'
quiz.explanation: Describing what you saw keeps the conversation calm and specific. Labels such as 'careless' or 'never' make people defensive.

quiz.question: Which is the best way to say no to an extra task when you are already busy?
options: 'No.'
'I'd like to help, but I can't before Friday. Could I start on Monday?'
'Yes, sure.' and then not do the task
'Why do I always get the extra work in this team?'
quiz.explanation: A polite no gives what you can't do, a reason or limit, and an alternative. Saying yes and not doing it is worse than an honest no.

quiz.question: Which apology follows the 'own it, fix it, prevent it' pattern?
options: 'Sorry sorry, my mistake, very sorry, it won't happen.'
'I'm sorry, I sent the wrong file. Here's the right one, and I'll double-check attachments from now on.'
'The system sent the wrong file, not me.'
'Sorry if you were confused.'
quiz.explanation: A good apology takes responsibility, fixes the problem and explains how you will stop it happening again. Blaming others or 'sorry if you were confused' avoids responsibility.

quiz.question: Which sentence is a polite conditional offer in a negotiation?
options: 'Confirm by Friday or we cancel your order.'
'We will give free delivery, maybe, if possible, perhaps.'
'If you confirm by Friday, we can include free delivery.'
'Free delivery is never possible for anyone.'
quiz.explanation: 'If you..., we can...' links what you offer to what you need. It is polite and it moves the negotiation forward.

quiz.question: Why can too many softeners be a problem?
options: Because softeners are grammatically wrong in English e-mails
Because English readers prefer very direct orders in all cases
Because softeners make an e-mail too short
The reader may not understand what you actually want
quiz.explanation: One softener is polite. Several ('maybe, if possible, perhaps') hide the request and leave the reader unsure what to do.

quiz.question: Which sentence is an I-statement for raising a problem?
options: 'You always send the data late and ruin the deadline.'
'Your team is the reason we miss every deadline.'
'Why can't you ever do anything on time?'
'I'm worried about the deadline, because the data arrived late twice this month.'
quiz.explanation: An I-statement explains your concern and the reason without attacking the other person, so they are more likely to listen and help.

quiz.question: A buyer's offer is lower than you can accept. Which response is most polite and useful?
options: 'That's a little lower than we can manage. Is there any flexibility on the quantity?'
'That price is a joke.'
'No. Final price. Take it or leave it.'
'Okay, we accept.' even though it is below your limit
quiz.explanation: Softened disagreement plus a question keeps the conversation open and looks for a solution. Accepting below your limit creates a bigger problem later.

bank.question: A visiting trainer from Dubai asks Ayesha, 'So, tell me a bit about yourself.' Which reply best combines a natural introduction with the 'answer plus one' habit?
options: 'Myself Ayesha. BBA completed. Looking for job.'
'I'm Ayesha. I've just finished my BBA and I'm looking for a marketing role. What brings you to Lahore?'
'My good name is Ayesha Malik and I am a BBA graduate from Lahore, sir.'
'Ayesha. Why do you ask?'
bank.explanation: It uses 'I'm...', gives a little background and a goal, and hands the conversation back with a question. The other replies are translated, too short or defensive.

bank.question: Which phrase is a direct translation from Urdu that may confuse an international colleague?
options: 'He is my cousin.'
'He is my cousin brother.'
'He's my older brother.'
'She's my cousin from Multan.'
bank.explanation: English uses 'cousin' for both male and female cousins, so 'cousin brother' sounds odd to many international listeners.

bank.question: At a work lunch, a new colleague from abroad asks Hamza how much he earns. What is the most polite way to handle it?
options: Tell them the exact figure, because refusing to answer would be impolite
Tell them firmly that the question is rude and walk away
Smile, give a light non-answer and change topic: 'Oh, enough for biryani on Fridays! How are you finding Karachi so far?'
Ask them how much they earn first and compare the two numbers
bank.explanation: Salary is a personal topic for most people. A friendly non-answer and a new, safe topic keep the relationship warm without sharing private information.

bank.question: Bilal speaks slowly, makes two small grammar mistakes and has a clear Pakistani accent, but the buyer understands every point. According to this course, how should he judge his performance?
options: As a success: he was clear and understood, and he can polish details over time
As a failure, because any grammar mistake at all makes him look unprofessional to buyers
As a failure, because he should have sounded like a native speaker
As a success only if the buyer did not notice his accent
bank.explanation: The goal is clear, polite communication. An accent is normal, and small mistakes matter much less than being understood. Practice will polish the rest.

bank.question: Which plan is most likely to build Ayesha's speaking confidence over a month?
options: One three-hour grammar study session on the last Sunday of the month
Waiting to speak until she has memorised a full dictionary of business words
Ten minutes of speaking practice every day, moving up the confidence ladder step by step
Only reading English novels silently, with no speaking practice at all
bank.explanation: Speaking is a skill built by short, regular practice. Daily low-pressure steps work better than rare long sessions or silent study alone.

bank.question: A colleague says, 'Thank you so much for covering my shift!' Which reply sounds most natural?
options: 'Mention not.'
'You're welcome. Happy to help.'
'Same to you.'
'It's okay, okay.'
bank.explanation: 'You're welcome' or 'No problem' are the standard replies to thanks. 'Mention not' is a translation that many international speakers do not use, and 'Same to you' answers wishes, not thanks.

bank.question: Which pair of small-talk questions is the best mix for meeting someone new at a work event?
options: 'How do you know the organisers?' then a follow-up on their answer
'Are you married?' then 'Why not?'
'Which party did you vote for?' then 'Why?'
'How old are you?' then 'How much is your rent?'
bank.explanation: An open, safe question followed by a follow-up on the other person's answer builds a real conversation. The other pairs are personal or divisive.

bank.question: Ayesha is updating her CV. Which sentence is correct?
options: I am working at this bank since 2021.
I have been working at this bank for 2021.
I have been working at this bank since 2021.
I am working at this bank from the year 2021 onwards.
bank.explanation: For an action that started in the past and continues now, use the present perfect continuous with 'since' and a starting point.

bank.question: Find the sentence with no mistakes.
options: She doesn't knows the answer, and she want to ask her manager.
She doesn't know the answer, and she wants to ask her manager.
She don't know the answer, and she is wanting to ask her manager.
She is not knowing the answer, and she wants to ask the her manager.
bank.explanation: After 'doesn't' use the base verb (know); 'she wants' takes -s; and state verbs such as know and want are not normally used in the -ing form.

bank.question: Hamza writes: 'I have submitted the form yesterday.' What is the problem?
options: 'Submitted' should be 'submit' after 'have'.
There is no problem; the sentence is correct.
'Yesterday' is a finished time, so it needs the past simple: 'I submitted the form yesterday.'
It should be 'I am submitting the form yesterday.'
bank.explanation: When you name a finished time such as yesterday, last week or in 2023, English uses the past simple, not the present perfect.

bank.question: Which sentence uses articles correctly?
options: He is an engineer at a factory in Sialkot, and the factory makes footballs.
He is engineer at factory in Sialkot, and factory makes the footballs.
He is an engineer at an factory in Sialkot, and a factory makes footballs.
He is the engineer at the a factory in Sialkot, and factory makes footballs.
bank.explanation: Use 'an' before the job (engineer), 'a' for the first mention of the factory, and 'the' when both people now know which factory. 'Footballs' in general needs no article.

bank.question: Which sentence has no preposition mistake?
options: We discussed about the plan and she explained me the changes.
We discussed the plan and she explained the changes to me.
We discussed on the plan and she explained to me about the changes.
We discussed about the plan and she explained the changes to me.
bank.explanation: 'Discuss' takes no preposition, and 'explain' needs 'to' before the person: 'explain something to someone'.

bank.question: A buyer keeps hearing 'iskool' when Bilal means 'school' and 'isteshun' for 'station'. What habit should Bilal practise?
options: Speaking more loudly so the extra vowel is not noticed
Adding an extra vowel at the end of each word as well
Starting the word directly with a long 's' sound, with no vowel in front
Avoiding all words that begin with s
bank.explanation: Many Urdu speakers add a vowel before s-clusters such as sk, st and sp. Starting with a long 'sss' sound removes it.

bank.question: Which question is correct?
options: Could you tell me what time does the train leave?
Could you tell me what time leaves the train?
What time the train leaves?
Could you tell me what time the train leaves?
bank.explanation: In an indirect question after 'Could you tell me...', use normal sentence order (subject then verb) and no 'does'. A direct question would be 'What time does the train leave?'

bank.question: Bilal answers the office phone. Which opening is most professional?
options: 'Hello, yes, tell me.'
'Noor Textiles. What?'
'Hello? Hello? Who is speaking there?'
'Good afternoon, Noor Textiles, Bilal speaking. How can I help you?'
bank.explanation: Greeting, company name and your own name tell callers they have the right place and who they are talking to.

bank.question: A caller spells her surname 'B-E-D-D-O-E-S' too fast. Which response is best?
options: 'Okay, got it,' and write down whatever you think you heard
'Your name is too difficult, I'll call you madam.'
'Please spell it in Urdu so I can understand.'
'Sorry, could you spell that again slowly? Was that B for Bravo, then D for Delta?'
bank.explanation: Asking for the spelling again and checking with the spelling alphabet removes confusion between letters such as B, D and P.

bank.question: Which reply to 'Would you mind sending the report today?' correctly means 'Yes, I'll do it'?
options: 'Yes, I would mind. I'll send it by 5 p.m.'
'Yes, I mind it. I'll send it by 5 p.m.'
'I would mind to send it by 5 p.m.'
'Not at all. I'll send it by 5 p.m.'
bank.explanation: 'Would you mind' asks whether it is a problem for you. 'Not at all' means it is no problem, so you agree.

bank.question: Which request is most suitable for asking a senior director, whom you don't know well, to review your proposal?
options: 'I was wondering if you might have time to look at my proposal this week.'
'Review my proposal this week, please.'
'You must look at my proposal this week.'
'Can you look at my proposal now? It's urgent.'
bank.explanation: With a senior person you don't know well, the most tentative form, 'I was wondering if you might...', is respectful and leaves room for them to say when they can.

bank.question: A caller gives the number 0321 4455 678. Which way of reading it back is clearest?
options: In small groups with pauses, for example 'oh-three-two-one... four-four, five-five... six-seven-eight'
As one huge number: 'three hundred twenty-one million...'
As fast as possible in one breath so the caller does not wait
Only the last four digits, because the rest is the same for everyone
bank.explanation: Phone numbers are read digit by digit in small groups. Pauses help the listener check each group.

bank.question: Ms Clarke from Leeds needs the revised price list for order 4471 before Thursday and asks for a call back. Bilal's manager is out. Which message to the manager is complete?
options: 'A lady from England called. Please call back.'
'Rebecca called about prices.'
'Order 4471 problem. Urgent.'
'Ms Rebecca Clarke, Clarke Home, Leeds, called at 4:30. Needs the revised price list for order 4471 before Thursday. Please call her back on the number below.'
bank.explanation: A complete message includes who called, from where, when, why, the deadline and how to reach them. The others leave the manager guessing.

bank.question: Why can 'Kindly revert immediately' sound rude, even though it contains 'kindly'?
options: Because 'kindly' is a rude word in British English and should never be used
It is still an order, and 'immediately' adds pressure, so the polite word does not soften it much
Because e-mails must never contain the word 'immediately' for legal reasons
Because it is too long and should just be 'Revert.'
bank.explanation: A request phrased as a question with a reasonable deadline, such as 'Could you reply by 3 p.m.?', is softer than an order with 'kindly' added. 'Revert' may also confuse international readers.

bank.question: In a meeting, Ayesha wants to show she agrees with a colleague and add an idea. Which sentence is correct and natural?
options: 'I am agree with Sara, and I want to add one point.'
'I am agreeing with Sara and adding one point.'
'Sara is right, and also one more thing is there.'
'I agree with Sara, and I'd like to add one point about timing.'
bank.explanation: 'Agree' is a verb and needs no 'am'. 'I'd like to add...' is a polite way to join in with an extra point.

bank.question: A colleague keeps talking over Bilal before he can finish. Which response is best?
options: Stop talking and say nothing for the rest of the meeting
'Let me finish na! You always do this to me in every meeting!'
'Could I just finish my point? Then I'd love to hear what you think.'
Raise his voice and keep talking louder until the colleague finally stops
bank.explanation: A calm request to finish, plus an offer to listen, protects your turn without starting an argument.

bank.question: Which answer to 'Tell me about yourself' is best for a customer service role at a Karachi bank?
options: A five-minute account of school, family and hobbies, in date order
One sentence: 'I am Hamza, I am hard working.'
A word-for-word reading of the CV the interviewer already has
A 75-second answer: current studies, a part-time job helping customers and why this role fits
bank.explanation: A focused answer covers present, relevant past and future, linked to the job, in about 60 to 90 seconds.

bank.question: Hamza's STAR answer is: 'There was a project. It was hard. We did a lot of work. It was good.' What is the main weakness?
options: There is no clear task, his own actions are missing and the result is vague
It uses the past tense, which interviewers do not like
It is far too long and detailed for a short answer in a job interview
It mentions a project, which interviewers do not want to hear about
bank.explanation: A strong STAR answer states the task, describes what 'I' did step by step and gives a clear result. Vague words such as 'a lot' and 'good' tell the interviewer nothing.

bank.question: Which result statement fits best at the end of a STAR answer?
options: 'It was a very good result and everyone was very, very happy with it.'
'We finished a week early, our tutor used our app as an example, and I learned to plan with weekly check-ins.'
'The result was that the project finished, as projects do.'
'Results are not important; only effort matters.'
bank.explanation: A good result is specific and honest, and it often includes what you learned. Vague praise gives the interviewer nothing to remember.

bank.question: In an online interview, Ayesha hears a question with a word she doesn't know: 'How would you measure the ROI of a campaign?' What is the best response?
options: Pretend the connection has dropped and rejoin the call later
Answer with a long description of her favourite campaign, hoping it fits
'Just to check, by ROI do you mean the return on investment, how much we gain compared with what we spend?' then answer
Say 'I didn't get you' and wait silently
bank.explanation: Checking the meaning in your own words is professional and calm. It also shows the interviewer that you think before you answer.

bank.question: Which weakness answer is likely to impress an interviewer most?
options: 'Honestly, I don't think I have any real weaknesses that would matter in this job.'
'I'm a perfectionist and I just care too much about my work.'
'I get angry easily, but only with people who deserve it.'
'I used to find it hard to say no, so now I check my deadlines before accepting extra work and offer another date if needed.'
bank.explanation: It names a real, manageable weakness and shows concrete action to improve. Cliches or no weakness at all sound rehearsed, and anger is a serious concern.

bank.question: Which sentence opens a presentation most clearly?
options: 'Good morning. Today I'll cover three things: our new range, the sales figures and the next steps.'
'Okay, so, basically, I will just start now, I think.'
'This is slide one. It has our logo.'
'Sorry, I'm not very good at English, so please forgive my mistakes.'
bank.explanation: A greeting and a short map of the talk help listeners follow. Apologising for your English at the start lowers confidence for no reason.

bank.question: A chart shows prices staying the same from January to June. Which sentence is correct?
options: 'Prices rose sharply from January to June.'
'Prices remained steady by January to June.'
'Prices remained steady from January to June.'
'Prices are remaining steady since January to June.'
bank.explanation: 'Remain steady' describes no change, and 'from... to...' gives the period. 'By' is for the amount of a change.

bank.question: Costs were 80,000 rupees in March and 60,000 rupees in April. Which sentence is correct?
options: 'Costs fell by 20,000 rupees to 60,000 rupees in April.'
'Costs fell to 20,000 rupees by 60,000 rupees in April.'
'Costs rose by 20,000 rupees to 60,000 rupees in April.'
'Costs have fallen by 20,000 rupees to 60,000 rupees last April.'
bank.explanation: The change was a fall of 20,000 (by) to a new level of 60,000 (to). With a finished time such as 'last April', the past simple is needed, not the present perfect.

bank.question: Bilal says: 'We deliver in six weeks, not ten.' Which word should he stress to make his point land?
options: 'six'
'We'
'in'
'weeks'
bank.explanation: The contrast between six and ten is the message, so the stress belongs on 'six'. Stressing the key word guides listeners to what matters.

bank.question: Which sentence describes a benefit rather than a feature?
options: 'Your shops will get fewer returns and more repeat customers.'
'Our sheets use long-staple cotton and a tighter weave.'
'Our factory in Faisalabad has thirty modern looms running day and night.'
'The sheets come in five colours and three sizes.'
bank.explanation: A benefit describes what the listener gains. Features describe the product or the company; they become persuasive when you link them to benefits.

bank.question: During Q&A, a buyer asks about a certification Bilal is not sure the company holds. What is the best response?
options: 'Yes, we have all certifications.' to keep the buyer interested
'That question is not relevant to today's presentation.'
'I want to give you an accurate answer, so I'll confirm with our compliance team and e-mail you by tomorrow.'
'I think maybe yes, probably, most likely we have it.'
bank.explanation: Claiming a certification you are unsure of is dishonest and risky. A specific promise to confirm keeps trust and the sale alive.

bank.question: Which group of phrases shows clear signposting from start to finish?
options: 'Okay...' / 'And then...' / 'Finished.'
'Today I'll cover...' / 'Let's move on to...' / 'To sum up...'
'Basically...' / 'Actually...' / 'So yeah...'
'Next slide.' / 'Next slide.' / 'Last slide.'
bank.explanation: Clear signposts tell the audience where the talk is going, when a new section starts and when you are concluding.

bank.question: Which e-mail opening is clearest and most professional for a client you have not met?
options: 'Dear Ms Rahman, I'm writing to confirm the delivery date for your order.'
'Respected Madam, Hope this finds you in the pink of health. I wanted to say that...'
'Hi dear, quick thing.'
'To whom it may concern, kindly do the needful.'
bank.explanation: 'Dear Ms...' is standard and the first sentence states the purpose. Very formal or vague openings delay the message and may sound old-fashioned or unclear to international readers.

bank.question: Ayesha writes: 'PFA the file. Kindly do the needful and revert ASAP.' Which rewrite is best for a client abroad?
options: 'Please find the attached file and do the needful as soon as possible.'
'FILE ATTACHED. APPROVE NOW.'
'Kindly revert on the attached at your earliest convenience.'
'I've attached the design. Could you approve it by Wednesday, so we can print on Thursday?'
bank.explanation: The best rewrite says what is attached, the exact action, the deadline and the reason. The others keep vague local phrases or shout.

bank.question: Which is the best way to soften bad news without hiding it?
options: 'Maybe, if possible, perhaps the shipment might possibly be a little bit delayed.'
'The shipment is late. Deal with it.'
Not mentioning the delay and hoping the client doesn't notice
'I'm afraid the shipment will be two days late. It will now arrive on Thursday.'
bank.explanation: One softener ('I'm afraid') plus clear facts is kind and honest. Too many softeners hide the message, and hiding the delay destroys trust.

bank.question: A team lead tells Hamza, 'Your summary was unclear.' Which response best shows he is receiving feedback well?
options: 'Sorry, sorry, very sorry, it won't happen again, sorry.'
'Thanks for telling me. Could you show me which part was unclear, so I can fix it?'
'My summary was clear. Maybe you didn't read it properly.'
'Okay.' and change nothing
bank.explanation: Thanking the person and asking for a specific example shows openness and makes it possible to improve. Repeated apologies, defensiveness and silence do not.

bank.question: Bilal's manager allows at most five per cent off for orders of 500 sets or more. A buyer asks for ten per cent on 300 sets. Which reply is best?
options: 'Okay, ten per cent is fine for you.'
'I'm afraid ten per cent isn't possible on 300 sets. However, if you order 500, we can offer five per cent. Would that work?'
'No. Not possible. Final.'
'Please tell me what discount you think is fair and I'll try.'
bank.explanation: It says no clearly, stays within the limits Bilal is allowed and offers a conditional alternative. Agreeing to unauthorised terms or a flat 'no' both damage the deal.

bank.question: Which sentence is the best I-statement for raising a problem with a colleague who sends data late?
options: 'You are always late and you are ruining this project for everyone.'
'I'm worried we'll miss the client deadline, because the data has arrived late twice this month. Can we agree a cut-off time?'
'Everyone in the team is unhappy with you.'
'I feel you are lazy.'
bank.explanation: A good I-statement names your concern, the specific facts and a request. 'I feel you are lazy' starts with 'I' but is still a personal label, not an I-statement about the problem.

bank.question: At the end of a phone negotiation, both sides agree on 500 sets with delivery in six weeks. What should Bilal do next?
options: Nothing, because a phone agreement is enough for everyone to remember
Wait for the buyer to write first, so he does not look too eager
Send a short e-mail: 'Just to confirm what we agreed today: 500 sets, delivery in six weeks.'
Send a long e-mail repeating the whole conversation word for word
bank.explanation: A short written summary confirms the agreement and catches any misunderstanding early, before goods or money move.
